basics.name: TRIZ Effects Database (Oxford Creativity), written and maintained by Andrew Martin
basics.url: https://wbam2244.dns-systems.net/EDB/index.php (the database itself; opened over https, since the plain-http address the Oxford Creativity page links to was blocked here). Landing page: https://www.triz.co.uk/triz-effects-database (opened). Help page: https://wbam2244.dns-systems.net/EDB/EDBHelpGeneral.html (opened)
basics.resource_type: interactive tool (free web lookup that answers 'how do I <do something> to <something>?' questions with a list of physical effects and devices)
basics.cost: Free. No sign-up, no login, no adverts. The author says it has 'no barriers to use (no signing up, signing in, adverts or invoices)'
basics.license: No open licence. Oxford Creativity's website terms reserve all copyright and forbid republishing or redistributing material from the site. The database runs on a separate host with no licence notice, so treat its descriptions as all rights reserved [uncertain]. Linking to the tool is fine. The effect names are general scientific terms that anyone can use, and most entries link to Wikipedia (CC BY-SA), which is the better thing to quote
basics.year: Built by Andrew Martin over 'more than 20 years' in his own time. Went live on the Oxford Creativity website in October 2011 (Martin, 'Brewing Free Beer: Using Ideality to develop a Free-to-use TRIZ Effects Database', Procedia Engineering 131:312-326, 2015). Content updates have continued since then. The date of the latest content update is not shown anywhere [uncertain]
basics.access_barrier: none (runs in any browser; queries are sent as form POSTs)
basics.image_license: Not applicable: the results are text only, with no images, diagrams or animations. Images on the linked Wikipedia pages carry their own Commons licences
basics.authority_level: educator (a TRIZ consultancy and training firm; one expert's curated list, which he says is based on analysis of patents; not peer-reviewed or an official standard). The design process behind the database is described in a peer-reviewed conference paper (Procedia Engineering, 2015)

coverage.covers: Physical phenomena ('effects') and simple devices that can perform a given function, such as holding, joining, moving, rotating, constraining, heating or separating a solid, divided solid (powder or granules), liquid, gas or field. A full sweep of all 175 Function queries (35 verbs x 5 object types) on 2026-09-25 returned 881 distinct effects, 867 of them linked to Wikipedia. There are also 5 x 39 Parameter queries and 9 x 9 Transform (energy-conversion) queries. For connections the relevant queries are large: 'Join Solid' returns 132 suggestions, 'Hold Solid' 123, 'Constrain Solid' 101, 'Rotate Solid' 122, 'Move Solid' 237, 'Stabilise Position' 99 and 'Increase Friction' 76. The results mix everyday connection types (adhesive, cyanoacrylate, screw, pin, hook, knot, Velcro, wedge, welding, soldering, brazing, mechanical fastener) with mechanisms (ratchet, escapement, cam, worm drive, epicyclic gearing, rack and pinion, sun and planet gear, swashplate, Peaucellier-Lipkin linkage, Hart's inversor, hinge, gimbal), powered and smart-material effects (electromagnet, electropermanent magnet, solenoid, shape memory alloy and polymer, magnetorheological and electrorheological fluids, electroactive polymer, Johnsen-Rahbek effect) and exotic physics (Casimir effect, Meissner effect, optical tweezers, acoustic levitation)
coverage.organisation: By function, as a two-part question. First you choose one of 3 query types: Function (e.g. 'Move Liquid'), Parameter (e.g. 'Increase Temperature') or Transform (e.g. 'Transform Mechanical Energy to Thermal Energy'). Then you pick one button from each of two lists, a verb and an object (e.g. Join + Solid), and optionally filter to pure Effects, Applications or both. The result is an alphabetical list of effect names, each followed by a short description and sometimes an application note that is specific to the query. This works well for someone who doesn't know the terms, because the questions are plain verbs ('Hold', 'Join', 'Rotate', 'Constrain'). The weakness is the output: 100 to 240 unranked suggestions with no grouping, so a beginner can't tell a practical fastener from an exotic lab effect
coverage.scope_match: medium: it isn't a catalogue of connection types, and most of its entries are physics rather than hardware. But its function-first questions ('How do I hold / join / constrain / rotate a solid?') are exactly the kind of entry point the project's flow chart needs. Its answers also name many in-scope types (ratchet, escapement, worm drive, epicyclic gearing, wedge, electropermanent magnet, solenoid, shape-memory alloy, gecko-type dry adhesive, hook-and-loop, knot), as well as a few odd, clever ideas worth mining (Johnsen-Rahbek electroadhesion, magnetorheological fluid clamping, tensegrity, origami)
coverage.taxonomy_used: TRIZ function-object-effect scheme. 3 top-level query modes: Function (35 verbs: Absorb, Accumulate, Bend, Break Down, Change Phase, Clean, Compress, Concentrate, Condense, Constrain, Cool, Deposit, Destroy, Detect, Dilute, Dry, Evaporate, Expand, Extract, Freeze, Heat, Hold, Join, Melt, Mix, Move, Orient, Produce, Protect, Purify, Remove, Resist, Rotate, Separate, Vibrate, each applied to 5 objects: Solid, Divided Solid, Liquid, Gas, Field); Parameter (5 verbs: Change, Decrease, Increase, Measure, Stabilise, applied to 39 parameters such as Force, Friction, Position, Orientation, Rigidity, Shape, Strength, Vibration); and Transform (9 x 9 energy types: acoustic, chemical, electrical, electromagnetic, kinetic, magnetic, mechanical, optical, thermal). Results are also tagged as pure Effects or Applications (the Effects / Applications / both filter)
coverage.example_types: ratchet; escapement; worm drive (self-locking gear); epicyclic (planetary) gearing; sun and planet gear; rack and pinion; cam; swashplate; Peaucellier-Lipkin linkage and Hart's inversor (straight-line linkages); gimbal; wedge; hook; knot; hook-and-loop (Velcro) and nano-Velcro; gecko-foot bristle array (dry adhesive); cyanoacrylate (superglue); electromagnet; electropermanent magnet (switchable magnet that holds with no power); solenoid; shape memory alloy; shape memory polymer; magnetorheological fluid and elastomer (field-controlled stiffening); Johnsen-Rahbek effect (electrostatic clamping); Halbach array; suction; tensegrity; rigid origami; fusible alloy (melts to release)
coverage.making_methods: None in particular. It's a general engineering and problem-solving aid based on patents, so it covers everything from mechanisms to chemistry and physics. There's nothing specific to 3D printing apart from '3D Printing' and 'Selective Laser Sintering' appearing as effects
coverage.item_count: 881 distinct effects reachable through the 175 Function queries (counted by a full sweep on 2026-09-25; 166 of those queries return at least one result, up to 237 each). Parameter and Transform queries may add a few more [uncertain]. The About page reports 636,736 queries answered all time, including 96,263 in the last year
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Partly, as bare names with a one- or two-sentence description and no design detail. One-way/ratchet: yes (Ratchet appears under Move, Rotate, Stabilise Position and Increase Friction). Indexing/detent: only indirectly (Escapement, Groove). Self-locking: yes, as Wedge, Worm Drive and Static Friction, although the entries don't explain self-locking. Hand-release only, torque-limiting (no clutch or slip entry) and over-centre (no toggle entry): no. Compliant: partly (Elasticity, Spring, Torsion Spring, Hinge, Rigid Origami, Auxetic Structures), but no flexure or compliant-mechanism entry. Print-in-place: no. Gear trains/gearboxes: partly (Gear, Epicyclic Gearing, Sun and Planet Gear, Worm Drive, Rack and Pinion, Pulley, Block and Tackle, Swashplate). Powered connectors: strong (Electromagnet, Electropermanent Magnet, Solenoid, Shape Memory Alloy, Magnetic Shape Memory, Electroactive Polymer, Electrorheological and Magnetorheological fluids, Johnsen-Rahbek electroadhesion, Electrostatics). Adhesive types: weak. Only generic 'Adhesive', 'Binder' and 'Cyanoacrylate' appear, plus processes (welding, soldering, brazing, sintering, photopolymerisation), and there's no guidance on which glue suits which material
coverage.entry_structure: Effect name (which links to Wikipedia or another web page for most effects), a 1-3 sentence plain description of the phenomenon and, for some query and effect pairs, a one-line application note (e.g. under Anisotropy: 'Self-assembling systems use anisotropic joints to facilitate correct selection and orientation of components'). No figures, no degrees of freedom, no design rules, no sources for individual entries
coverage.audience_level: professional (TRIZ practitioners, product engineers and people learning TRIZ); usable by a curious hobbyist

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium: the questions are very easy (pick a verb and a thing), and the descriptions are short and mostly plain. But the answers are long, unranked alphabetical lists that mix everyday hardware with advanced physics (e.g. Casimir effect next to Chain under 'Join Solid'), with no guidance on practicality, cost or difficulty. The author's own paper notes users now ask 'can they be filtered in some way?'
usefulness.gaps: No pictures. No ranking or practicality rating (everyday, maker-feasible or lab-only). No distinction between permanent, removable and adjustable joints. No design rules or sizes. No materials or making-method filter. No special-behaviour vocabulary (torque-limiting, over-centre, hand-release, detent). Adhesives aren't broken down by chemistry or material. Results can't be bookmarked (POST form, no per-query or per-effect URL). Many important connection types are missing entirely: a name search of all 881 Function results found no snap fit, bayonet, press fit, threaded insert, circlip, dovetail, flexure, latch, clutch, brake, detent, toggle/over-centre, buckle or rivet (only generic 'Mechanical Fastener', 'Screw' and 'Pin')
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: low: queries are POST-only, so there's no stable URL for a query result or a single effect. Only the start page (https://wbam2244.dns-systems.net/EDB/index.php) and help page can be linked. For single entries, link to the Wikipedia page that the database itself points to instead
usefulness.reusable_data: scrape-only: there's no API, download or dataset, but the whole Function set can be collected with 175 simple form POSTs (as done for the counts here). The list of effects is Oxford Creativity's own curation, and the site terms forbid republishing, so use it as a source of ideas and cross-check names, not as a dataset to copy. The function verbs and object classes are generic TRIZ vocabulary and free to reuse
usefulness.maintained: Online and working on 2026-09-25 (queries answered; 198 queries in the previous 24 hours according to the About page). The landing page on triz.co.uk (copyright 2026) still promotes it. The host is an odd shared-hosting domain (wbam2244.dns-systems.net) rather than triz.co.uk, which is a link-rot risk. Wayback Machine copies weren't checked because archive.org rate-limited the request [uncertain]
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Verb + object question as the first step of the flow chart: 'What do you want it to do?' (Hold / Join / Constrain / Rotate / Move / Orient / Stabilise position / Increase friction) x 'to what?' (a solid part, a powder, a liquid, a gas). This maps directly onto a beginner's own words. (2) Three entry modes: by function, by changing a parameter (make it stiffer, stop it moving, increase grip) and by energy conversion (turn electrical into mechanical, which suits powered connectors and actuators). (3) An Effects vs Applications filter, which is like the project splitting 'principles' (friction, magnetism, elasticity) from 'devices' (cam cleat, ratchet). (4) Query-specific one-line application notes that explain why an effect answers this particular question. (5) Linking each result out to Wikipedia for depth instead of rewriting it. (6) Learning from its weakness: rank or group results (everyday / maker-friendly / specialist), because long flat lists overwhelm users
usefulness.design_rules_given: No. No numbers, clearances, strengths or torques
usefulness.terminology_value: medium: useful for finding the proper physics or device name behind a vague idea (e.g. electropermanent magnet, Johnsen-Rahbek effect, magnetorheological elastomer, Peaucellier-Lipkin linkage, Stockbridge damper), and each name comes with a Wikipedia link. No aliases, translations or maker slang. A few typos and encoding glitches (e.g. 'Govenor', the dash in 'Peaucellier-Lipkin' shown as a bad character)
usefulness.decision_support: Yes, a simple two-step selector with no scoring. Step 1: choose a query type (Function, Parameter or Transform). Step 2: choose one verb and one object from two sets of radio buttons (e.g. Join + Solid, or Stabilise + Position), plus an optional Effects / Applications / both filter, then submit. The output is an unranked alphabetical list of candidate effects, with counts shown (e.g. '132 suggestions for Join Solid'), each with a description and link. The user decides which suggestions are useful ('You will have to decide for yourself which (if any) of the suggested effects is useful'). There's no further filtering by material, size, cost, reversibility or feasibility, no comparison table and no follow-up questions
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Built on the TRIZ tradition of 'effects databases' begun by Altshuller's pointer-to-effects lists [uncertain]. The 2015 paper says the most comprehensive effects databases were commercial, and it set out to match them for free. Its effect descriptions are largely summaries of the matching Wikipedia articles, which it links to, so Wikipedia is the citable source for each effect. Overlaps with other free TRIZ effect lists (e.g. the MATRIZ knowledge base's 'Database of scientific effects' page, and Aulive's ProductionInspiration, which the TRIZ Consulting Group lists alongside it) and with Wikipedia's mechanism categories
